issue: A large government website launches on schedule but immediately becomes unusable for the vast majority of people trying to sign up
root_cause: According to widely reported post-incident analysis, the failure stemmed from broad organizational and process problems rather than a single technical bug: fragmented ownership across many contractors, insufficient end-to-end load testing before launch, and a lack of a single technical leader accountable for overall system integration and performance.
solution: A dedicated technical response team was brought in after launch to rebuild and stabilize the site over the following months, including consolidating technical decision-making and running realistic load tests that had been skipped before the original launch.
note: This is a well-known organizational/process failure rather than a single discrete technical incident; treat differently from other entries in evaluation since it may not fit a typical single-cause RCA pattern.

issue: After what looked like a routine operating-system package update, some customer application containers can no longer write to certain device paths
root_cause: An update to an upstream system package broke compatibility with other packages that had been deliberately pinned to specific versions for stability, and the resulting mismatch caused write permission failures to specific device paths that customer applications depended on.
solution: Rolled back or re-pinned the affected packages to restore compatible versions, restoring write access, and reviewed the update process to catch this kind of upstream breaking change before it reaches customer-facing infrastructure.
note: Brief public summary; verify against Heroku's own status/incident report before finalizing.

issue: Customers report their private repository data and account credentials appear to have been used by someone else, weeks after a routine-seeming platform update
root_cause: Private authentication tokens were leaked, which allowed unauthorized parties to retrieve data from internal databases, private repositories, and customer accounts; the public summary doesn't specify exactly how the tokens were leaked, only the scope of what became accessible as a result.
solution: Revoked and rotated the leaked tokens platform-wide, forced re-authentication for affected accounts, and notified customers whose private repository data or account information may have been accessed.
note: Brief public summary; this overlaps conceptually with well-documented OAuth-token incidents from other providers around the same period -- verify against Heroku's specific incident report before finalizing.

issue: An observability platform's own monitoring goes down repeatedly over eight-plus hours, undermining the team's ability to monitor the very outage they're fighting
root_cause: According to the company's own detailed public writeup, the ingest system (responsible for taking in customer telemetry data) failed repeatedly; root causes across the underlying incidents included capacity limits reached from fast company growth outpacing infrastructure scaling, compounding with each restart attempt before the underlying capacity issue was fully addressed.
solution: Scaled the ingest system's underlying capacity to match actual growth, and published a detailed internal review process afterward to catch this class of growth-outpacing-capacity issue earlier next time.

issue: An app crashes repeatedly and unpredictably, and the crash pattern is really hard to pin down because it doesn't correlate cleanly with any single deploy or traffic pattern
root_cause: A single malformed event (a "poison pill") in an asynchronous worker queue triggered an unhandled panic every time a worker tried to process it; because the queue kept retrying the same poison-pill event, it kept crashing new worker instances as they picked it up, and this combined poorly with the hosting infrastructure's process-restart behavior, making the actual source of the repeated crashes difficult to isolate at first.
solution: Identified and removed the poison-pill event from the queue to stop the crash loop, then added defensive handling so a single malformed event triggers a caught error and gets set aside for inspection rather than crashing the whole worker.

issue: A hardware-manufacturer's chips occasionally produce very slightly wrong answers on a specific class of math operation, discovered by an outside academic rather than internal testing
root_cause: A scripting bug caused certain entries to be omitted from a lookup table used by the chip's division logic, so a small set of specific division operations occasionally produced incorrect results; the bug wasn't caught internally because a mathematical proof of the divider's correctness rested on an incorrect assumption that all necessary table entries were present.
solution: Once identified, redesigned the affected chip revision to correct the divider logic and, after public pressure, offered replacements for affected chips even though the practical impact for most users was extremely rare.

issue: An admin tool's dropdown for selecting a targeting rule crashes the whole feature-flag management interface, but only for certain flag configurations
root_cause: A specific attribute selector used when defining flag-targeting rules had a bug that caused the web interface responsible for flag targeting to crash when that selector was used or displayed under certain conditions.
solution: Identified the specific attribute-selector bug and patched the targeting interface so it handles that condition without crashing, restoring normal flag-management functionality.
note: Brief public summary; verify against LaunchDarkly's own postmortem before finalizing.

issue: A single availability zone in a cloud region has problems, but the customer-facing application keeps running normally throughout
root_cause: An outage affecting one availability zone degraded resources hosted specifically in that zone; because the affected application was already architected to run across multiple availability zones rather than depending on just one, the zone-level outage didn't translate into customer-visible impact.
solution: Migrated/failed over the affected workloads to healthy availability zones as a standard, pre-planned response, avoiding any customer-visible disruption; no emergency remediation was needed beyond the multi-AZ architecture already in place.
note: This is presented as a resilience success story rather than a customer-facing incident -- useful as a contrasting example of good multi-AZ design, but may not fit a typical RCA training example the way a true outage would.

issue: SMS/voice-based alerting stops working for some customers, but the incident-management platform itself is otherwise healthy
root_cause: A third-party SMS/voice provider that the platform depends on for delivering notifications experienced its own outage, which was itself caused by a major cloud provider having regional infrastructure issues; the notification platform's own systems were healthy, but the downstream dependency it relies on for actually delivering the alert wasn't.
solution: Failed over to an alternate notification channel/provider where possible while the third-party SMS/voice provider's own outage was resolved by that provider, and reviewed how much the notification system depends on a single downstream provider without a built-in fallback.
note: Brief public summary; verify against PagerDuty's own status/blog post before finalizing.

issue: A platform-as-a-service's scheduled maintenance window runs far longer than planned, seemingly stuck rather than progressing
root_cause: A coordination service central to the platform's operation required loading more data during startup than it could handle within its configured limits, so it failed to boot properly during the planned maintenance window, stalling the maintenance rather than allowing it to proceed as scheduled.
solution: Adjusted the coordination service's startup data-handling limits (or reduced the data it needed to load at boot) so it could start successfully, then completed the originally planned maintenance.
note: Brief public summary; verify against Platform.sh's own postmortem before finalizing.

issue: Some customers suddenly can't log in or access their account at all, right after what internal teams considered a routine, low-risk security review update
root_cause: A policy change made as part of a standard, recurring security-controls review was intended to have a narrow, specific scope, but it inadvertently applied more broadly than intended, blocking legitimate access to resources -- including login -- for a subset of customers who shouldn't have been affected by the change at all.
solution: Identified the overly broad policy change and rolled it back to its intended, narrower scope, restoring login and resource access for affected customers.

issue: A chat platform's connection stability suddenly degrades after routine cache-infrastructure maintenance that was expected to be invisible to users
root_cause: Removing cache nodes as part of routine maintenance shifted more load onto a lightweight coordination component (a "witness" cluster) than it was sized to handle; that component became overloaded, and because other parts of the system depended on it for coordination, the overload cascaded into a broader service outage rather than staying contained to caching alone.
solution: Restored removed cache capacity (or added capacity to the witness cluster) to relieve the overload, then resized the witness cluster's capacity planning to account for load spikes during cache-related maintenance going forward.
note: Brief public summary; verify against Slack's own engineering blog before finalizing.

issue: A single slow or failing downstream service causes a much larger set of unrelated services to also become slow, well beyond what its actual usage would suggest
root_cause: A microservice that called a downstream dependency lacked exponential backoff in its retry logic; when the downstream dependency became slow or unavailable, the microservice kept retrying at a constant, aggressive rate rather than backing off, amplifying load on the already-struggling downstream service and causing the problem to cascade into a broader, more severe outage than the original issue alone would have caused.
solution: Added exponential backoff (and likely circuit-breaking) to the retry logic so that a struggling downstream dependency gets progressively less retry pressure instead of more, preventing this class of cascading amplification in the future.
note: Brief public summary; verify against Spotify's own engineering blog before finalizing.

issue: Merchants suddenly can't authenticate card transactions for about two hours, with no changes made to the payment system itself that day
root_cause: A cascading error originating in an adjacent, dependent service overloaded the merchant-authentication service that verifies transactions; the authentication service itself hadn't changed, but the load from the failing adjacent service was enough to degrade it, impacting merchants' ability to process transactions.
solution: Isolated the failing adjacent service to stop it from overloading the authentication service, and added load-shedding/circuit-breaking between the two services so a failure in one can no longer directly overload the other.
note: Brief public summary; verify against Square's own engineering blog before finalizing.

issue: Enabling a new feature for the entire user base at once accidentally knocks the whole site offline, even though the feature itself worked fine in smaller rollouts
root_cause: A new feature was enabled for all users simultaneously rather than through a gradual rollout; the resulting sudden spike in requests to load balancers was effectively indistinguishable from a self-inflicted denial-of-service attack, overwhelming infrastructure that had been sized for gradual adoption rather than an instant full-user-base switch-on.
solution: Disabled the feature for all users to relieve load, then re-enabled it through a proper gradual/staged rollout with load monitoring at each stage instead of an all-at-once launch.
note: Brief public summary; verify against Stack Exchange's own status blog before finalizing.

issue: One specific piece of user-generated content makes the whole site unhealthy, while every other page loads fine
root_cause: A regular expression used somewhere in request/content processing had a backtracking-heavy pattern that behaved fine for typical content but became extremely computationally expensive against one particular post's content, consuming so much CPU on the server handling it that health checks for that server began failing, eventually contributing to a broader service outage.
solution: Identified the specific expensive regular expression and rewrote it to avoid catastrophic backtracking, and added execution-time limits on user-content-driven pattern matching so a single expensive input can no longer threaten overall service health.
note: Brief public summary; verify against Stack Exchange's own status blog before finalizing.

issue: During a migration to a newer internal system, some users' profile information ends up visible in places it shouldn't be
root_cause: Old code from a legacy product was ported to a newer system without fully accounting for differences in how the two systems handled data visibility/scoping, resulting in some users' information being exposed in the new system in ways it hadn't been in the old one.
solution: Identified the visibility/scoping gap introduced during the port, corrected the access rules in the new system to match the intended (more restrictive) behavior, and audited what had actually been exposed before notifying affected users.
note: Brief public summary; verify against Stack Exchange's own status blog before finalizing.

issue: A backup encryption service silently stops functioning correctly over a period of days, with the local disk quietly filling up in the background
root_cause: A batch job that scans for and frees unused storage blocks hit a persistent condition where every retry to free certain specific blocks kept failing; rather than surfacing this as an alert, the job simply kept logging each failed attempt to a local log file that grew without any size limit, eventually filling the local filesystem and causing unrelated writes -- including the core service's own operation -- to fail once there was no disk space left.
solution: Manually deleted the oversized log file to free disk space and immediately restore service, then added both a size cap on the log file and proper alerting so a persistently failing cleanup job surfaces as an actionable alert instead of silently filling the disk.

issue: A gaming platform's desktop application, on a routine update, deletes every local file on the user's machine instead of just updating itself
root_cause: A bug in the desktop client's update/install logic caused it to delete the entire contents of local directories rather than just the files it was meant to manage; the bug had reportedly been reported by users through official channels months before it caused widespread damage, but wasn't triaged or prioritized in time to prevent the broader impact.
solution: Once the issue went viral on social media, the update was reverted/patched to stop the destructive deletion behavior, and the bug-triage process was reportedly reviewed given how long the original report had gone unaddressed.
note: Widely reported via social media/community channels rather than an official company postmortem; verify specifics before relying on this for evaluation.

issue: A stock brokerage's order-management system completely stops processing any orders after one unusual, oversized order comes through
root_cause: An order for a very large quantity of a low-priced stock was automatically split by the trading system into far more individual smaller trades than the order-management system's provider had ever encountered before at that scale; this unprecedented volume of split trades overwhelmed and collapsed the order-management system, which hadn't been tested against an order of that particular size and structure.
solution: Restored the order-management system and worked with the provider to add safeguards limiting how many individual trades a single order can be split into, or flagging unusually large orders for special handling before they reach the point of overwhelming the system.

issue: A brokerage's backup network connection to the stock exchange works, but unreliably, causing certain order types to fail intermittently for about an hour
root_cause: The primary leased line connection to the exchange failed, triggering activation of the backup leased line; the backup line itself operated sporadically rather than reliably, and certain order types (bracket and cover orders) that depended on consistent connectivity were affected by the backup line's intermittent behavior during that window.
solution: Restored the primary line once its issue was fixed, and adjusted order-placement and validation logic to explicitly account for leased-line unreliability going forward, though the underlying reliability of both the primary and backup lines was reportedly not fundamentally improved by the telecom providers afterward.

issue: A trading firm's automated system starts sending huge volumes of erratic, unintended orders across dozens of stocks the moment markets open, with no human trader involved
root_cause: A new software release was deployed to eight production servers, but one of the eight still had an old feature flag left enabled from a previous, retired testing tool. That flag reactivated a long-dormant, unused code path (an old order-testing feature) which began generating a flood of unintended live orders as soon as the market opened, since nothing distinguished that one server's stale configuration from the other seven until the erroneous orders were already executing.
solution: The firm had to identify which of the eight servers was misconfigured and halt/disable it, but by the time trading was stopped, tens of thousands of erroneous trades had already executed across many stocks; the financial losses were severe enough that the firm required emergency external funding to remain solvent.
note: No official internal postmortem from Knight Capital is publicly available; this account is reconstructed from the SEC's public administrative proceeding and widely-cited secondary analysis. Verify specifics against the SEC filing before final use.

issue: Payments start hard-failing for live customers within minutes of a major, publicly-streamed product launch, despite the same flow working fine in staging
root_cause: A certificate mismatch in the payment processing path caused payment requests to fail; the mismatch existed only in the production environment's certificate configuration and had not been present (or not been exercised) in staging, so pre-launch testing didn't catch it before the public launch traffic hit the real payment path.
solution: The team scrambled to identify the certificate mismatch during the live launch and corrected it to restore payment processing, then added checks specifically targeting this class of environment-specific certificate configuration difference so it would be caught in staging before any future launch.
